newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S-Russian space crew upbeat after collision.
newsitem.headline: U.S-Russian space crew upbeat after collision.

text.p: An American and two Russians, who are preparing to repair the damaged space station Mir, looked well and confident on Sunday in their first television link with Earth since their accident in orbit.

"When we had problems with light and air conditioning, we were killing time by eating," commander Vasily Tsibliyev said in reply to a question about reported problems with hot food after an unmanned cargo craft collided with Mir last Wednesday.
"Thank God, everything works fine now," he said with a smile to officials at Korolyov mission control, near Moscow.

Mir lost between 30 and 40 percent of its electric power potential after the cargo craft collided with it during a manual docking manoeuvre. The Spektr scientific module, which was already docked with Mir, was holed during the collision.

A spokeswoman for mission control said earlier on Sunday that Tsibliyev, flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin and British- born physicist Michael Foale were dismantling some secondary equipment in the crowded station to make room to put on their spacesuits when they carry out the planned repairs.
During the television link, which lasted about nine minutes, the crew took the camera around Mir to show some of the key points for the repair work, needed to restore the power supply.
"We have been trained for all sorts of imaginable and unimaginable incidents and of course some of the elements of our training will be used in the work ahead," Lazutkin said.

"When we had to fight the loss of pressure after the incident (last Wednesday), I realised at some point that I was working automatically, without thinking," he added. "That shows that the training was really solid."

Foale, 40, Tsibliyev, 43, and Lazutkin, 39, were due to check how the station's batteries were charging and to try to increase their oxygen supply. The spokeswoman said additional systems were being activated as Mir's batteries charged, including the station's toilet and the greenhouse.

The two Russians will don spacesuits to enter Spektr while Foale sits in the escape capsule for safety. They must install a modified hatch in Spektr's doorway so that cables can be connected to tap electricity from the module's solar arrays.
According to officials from the U.S. space agency NASA, if the hatch to Spektr cannot be resealed, the crew will have to abandon ship.

Vladimir Solovyov, who is responsible for flight coordination at mission control, said on Saturday a cargo craft would be launched on July 5 to take equipment to Mir. He expected the repairs to be done between July 10 and 14.

Despite a string of recent mishaps on Mir, NASA appears committed to sending astronauts to what is still the world's only space station. It is due to be replacedby the international station Alpha in the next few years.

"Our current plan is to continue the missions. If something came up to change that assessment, we would certainly look at it very seriously," Frank Culbertson, the veteran astronaut who runs NASA's joint missions with Mir, said.
Foale sounded optimistic about his space career. "Of course I will have more flights. I have vast experience now," he said in Russian and smiling when asked about his future plans.
"But even when things go wrong, it is great to work with these wonderful guys," he added.
